title: Interference: cutting the defender's line
summary: Drop a piece or pawn onto the line between a defender and what it defends.

steps.md:
**Interference** cuts a line: you place a piece (often with a threat or as a sacrifice) on a square between an enemy line piece and the thing it protects. The protected piece is then loose.

Recipe: (1) find an enemy piece that is defended **only** by a rook, bishop or queen from a distance; (2) look at the squares in between; (3) can one of your pieces land there with tempo, or so that capturing it is impossible or costly?
White to move. The b6-bishop is defended only by the queen on e6 along the sixth rank. The squares between them are c6 and d6. Your d1-rook can land on d6 **attacking the queen**.

steps.prompt: White to move. Cut the queen off from the bishop.
steps.explain: **26.Rd6!** attacks the queen and cuts its line to b6. The queen must move (26...Qxa2) and **27.Rxb6** wins the bishop. A rook move that both attacks and interferes.

steps.prompt: Black to move. The g5-knight is defended only by the queen on d2. Interfere with a pawn.
steps.explain: **21...e3!** The pawn lands on the d2-g5 diagonal and attacks the queen at the same time. After 22.Rxe3 the rook itself blocks the diagonal, so **22...Qxg5** wins the knight. 22.fxe3 Qxg5 is the same story, and 22.Qxe3?? Rxe3 drops the queen down the e-file.

steps.question: What makes a defender vulnerable to interference?
choices: It defends from far away along a line, with empty squares in between
It is a knight defending from close range
It is defended by a pawn
steps.explain: Only **line pieces** (R, B, Q) defending at a distance can be interfered with: a knight or pawn defends by jumping or touching and has no line to cut. The longer the line, the more squares you can drop a piece on.

steps.prompt: Black to move. White's queen has grabbed g7 and protects his a1-rook along the long diagonal. Interfere and attack at once.
steps.explain: **4...Bf6!** hits the queen and blocks the g7-a1 diagonal. The queen must flee (5.Qg3) and **5...Bxa1** wins the rook. Interference with tempo is the strongest form.

steps.prompt: Black to move. Independent exercise: White's a1-rook is defended only by the e5-queen.
steps.explain: **23...Bd4!** attacks the queen and cuts the e5-a1 diagonal; the bishop is protected by the d8-rook. After 24.Qe1 (the queen defends nothing on a1 because the b1-knight blocks the first rank) **24...Bxa1** wins the exchange.

steps.md:
**Typical errors.** (1) Interfering on a square where your piece is simply captured with no gain: check what the capture does. (2) Forgetting that the defender may have another route (a second line or a different defender). (3) Missing interference *against you*: before you rely on a long-range defender, ask whether a piece can be dropped between.

**Retrieval check.** Name the three-step recipe from the start of the lesson, then name which piece was cut off in each of the four puzzles.

sources: Yusupov, Build Up Your Chess 2 (Quality Chess, 2009), chapter on interference
